message.content:
Build a NEW marketing homepage concept for Nxeon at route `/newwebsitev8`. This is one of four concepts being built in parallel for a bake-off; yours must be visually unmistakable from the others.

## Your concept: v8 — "Arcade". Dark, maximalist, game-first.

Game servers are the owner's single most important product line, and this concept goes all-in on that audience. Poster-led, high-saturation, big confident type, card-heavy. Real game key art at large scale, treated like a premium storefront or a games-press feature spread rather than a SaaS page.

The other three concepts are restrained (a technical instrument, a light editorial piece, a product walkthrough). **Yours is the loud one** — but loud and *expensive*, not loud and cheap. The failure mode to avoid is "gamer website": no neon-on-black Rajdhani/Orbitron lettering, no angular clipped-corner panels, no RGB gradients on everything, no cyberpunk. Think a premium console storefront or a well-art-directed games magazine: rich, dense, confident, beautifully set.

- Use the real game key art heavily — portrait posters and 16:9 heroes both exist on disk.
- Interaction: tactile, physical-feeling cards. Pointer-tracked tilt with a light sheen, a draggable rail, a poster that lifts and reveals its plan details. Springy easing. Make picking a game feel good.
- Type: a display face with real personality at large sizes. NOT Inter, Geist, or Space Grotesk, and not a sci-fi/gamer face. Load via `next/font/google`.
- Ground stays dark, but pull colour from the game art itself rather than one global accent — let each title's poster tint its own card's glow.

## Repo context

- Root: `/opt/nxeon`. Next.js App Router, Tailwind v4, TypeScript. **Work directly in /opt/nxeon.**
- Create `app/newwebsitev8/layout.tsx`, `app/newwebsitev8/page.tsx`, `app/newwebsitev8/v8.css`, plus client components in that directory. **Touch no files outside `app/newwebsitev8/`** — three other agents are working in this same checkout in parallel.
- The layout must wrap children in `<div className="v8 ...">` and scope ALL your CSS under `.v8`. Import your css from the layout.
- Set `robots: { index: false, follow: false }` in the layout's `metadata`.
- Page should be a Server Component (`export const dynamic = "force-dynamic"`) passing real data into client components.

## Real data sources (use these — do not hardcode numbers)

- `db.gamePlan` — the important one: `gameFamily`, `ramMB`, `cpuCores`, `diskGB`, `slots`, `priceCents`, `active`. 42 active families. Cheapest tiers range roughly $5.38–$32.
- `db.gameMod.count({ where: { active: true, upstreamOk: true } })` — mod catalogue size. Also `findMany({ distinct: ["gameFamily"] })` to count families covered.
- `db.plan` — VPS plans (`priceCents`, `active`).
- Regions: `regionsFrom` from `@/lib/nx/catalog` with `db.node.findMany({ where: { enabled: true }, select: { id: true, region: true } })` → exactly TWO: Singapore and Germany. `CUSTOMER_REGION_LABELS` from `@/lib/node-regions`.
- Game metadata: `GAME_DISPLAY` (display names), `GAME_ART_SLUG` (art filename slugs — note `arkasa` maps to `ark-asa`, `sdtd` to `7-days-to-die`, `projectzomboid` to `project-zomboid`), `GAME_GENRES` from `@/lib/games`; `GAME_URL_SLUG` from `@/lib/marketing/gameLocationLandings` for per-game links (`/{GAME_URL_SLUG[fam]}-server-hosting`).
- `db` is `import { db } from "@/lib/db"`.

## HONESTY CONSTRAINTS — hard requirements

- **No testimonials, reviews, ratings, or player counts.** `Review` and `Testimonial` tables are empty. Invent none. No Google/Trustpilot widgets. No "12,000 servers deployed" style figures.
- **No invented statistics.** No customer counts, no data-centre counts, no continents. Exactly TWO regions.
- **Game names and key art are third-party trademarks.** Present them as titles Nxeon hosts — never imply endorsement, partnership, or official status from any game studio.
- Pre-approved claims: `99.99% network`, `online in 47 seconds`.
- Prices and slot counts must come from the database.

## Known traps in this codebase

- **Do NOT export an object-of-components from a `"use client"` module and read properties off it in a Server Component** (`export const Icon = {...}` then `<Icon.x/>` server-side) — resolves to `undefined` and React throws "Element type is invalid". Shared SVG icons go in a module with NO `"use client"`.
- `.v8 .card { position: relative }` (specificity 0,2,0) **beats** Tailwind's `lg:absolute` (0,1,0). Put positioning utilities on a wrapper if they must win.
- Grids stretch rows to the tallest sibling; use `content-start`/`items-start` or you get large dead bands.
- A drag-vs-click threshold below ~8px makes ordinary clicks register as drags and swallows them — this has been a real bug in this repo. If you build a draggable rail, use a threshold around 40px and don't call `setPointerCapture` until movement crosses it.
- `public/logos/caddy.svg` is 0 bytes — don't reference it.
- Keep the page readable **at rest** — never park content at `opacity: 0` waiting on a scroll observer. Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.

## Assets

- `public/games/art/<GAME_ART_SLUG[fam].poster>_poster.jpg` — portrait key art (3:4).
- `public/games/art/<GAME_ART_SLUG[fam].hero>_hero.jpg` — 16:9 key art.
- `public/logos/minecraft.svg`, `counterstrike.svg`, `steam.svg` — a few game logos.
- `/logo.png`, `/nx-mark.png` — the real brand marks. Never invent a logo.
- `public/nx/art/gamepad.webp` — portal game illustration.

## Process

Two-pass design process: write a short design plan first (palette as 4-6 named hex values, 2+ typefaces with roles, layout concept), then **review it against the concept** and revise anything that reads like the generic "gamer site" or generic SaaS default, noting what you changed. Then write code.

Build the hero plus 3-4 sections. Fewer, better sections.

## Rules

- `npx tsc --noEmit` from `/opt/nxeon` must pass when you're done. Other agents are editing the same checkout, so errors under `app/newwebsitev5|v6|v7/**` are not yours — ignore them and confirm your own files are clean.
- **Do NOT run any git command. Do NOT commit, branch, or stage anything.** Leave your files on disk; the parent commits all four together.
- **Do NOT deploy and do NOT run `npm run build`.**
- Report back: what you built (file list), design plan + what self-review changed, anything you couldn't verify.

133	 * these are the ONLY ports Docker actually exposes off the container, so they

226	  stationeers: { port: 27500, protocol: "tcp" }, // image maps 27500 as both tcp+udp (web-interface tcp); 27015/udp is query
227	  // Eco's GameServerPort (3000) is UDP, not TCP — verified live 2026-09-07 off a
228	  // running EcoServer's own /proc/net (udp:3000 bound, no tcp:3000 at all). Only
229	  // the WebServer (3001) and RCON (3002) are TCP. The old `tcp` here made the
230	  // provisioning health check connect to a port nothing ever listens on, so every
231	  // Eco order failed the check even once the server did start.
232	  eco: { port: 3000, protocol: "udp" }, // 3001/tcp is EcoWebServer, 3002/tcp is RCON
233	  empyrion: { port: 30000, protocol: "udp" }, // no tcp port mapped (30000-30003/udp range)
234	  // plutoniumt4: confirmed against the community Plutainer image's own T4 example
235	  // (`-p 28960:28960/udp`, see prisma/seed-plutonium.ts) and against Plutonium's
236	  // own Linux-hosting guides, which forward 28960-28961/udp for the game itself.
237	  // No TCP port is mapped for the game server (the optional FastDL HTTP port,
238	  // 8000/tcp, is a customer-configured add-on, not part of the base container).
239	  plutoniumt4: { port: 28960, protocol: "udp" },
240	  // plutoniumt5/t6/iw5: confirmed against Plutainer's own games.md docs
241	  // (github.com/Ayymoss/Plutainer/blob/main/docs/games.md) — T5 shares T4's
242	  // 28960/udp game port (same IW3-derived engine lineage); T6 (Black Ops 2)
243	  // defaults to 4976/udp (also matches the community thejcpalma/aio-plutonium-t6
244	  // image's SERVER_PORT default, independent corroboration); IW5 (MW3) defaults
245	  // to 27016/udp (net_port), matching both Plutainer's docs and the Steam
246	  // "Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3 - Dedicated Server" tool's documented port.
247	  // No TCP port mapped for any of the three — same base-container shape as T4.
248	  plutoniumt5: { port: 28960, protocol: "udp" },
249	  plutoniumt6: { port: 4976, protocol: "udp" },
250	  plutoniumiw5: { port: 27016, protocol: "udp" },
251	};
252	
253	/**
254	 * The families whose {@link GAME_PORT} entry is deliberately NOT the port a
255	 * player's own game client connects to — mapped to the port that actually is.
256	 *
257	 * `GAME_PORT` is a HEALTH-CHECK map. Where an image exposes a TCP port at all it
258	 * prefers that one, because "a TCP handshake is verifiable with a plain connect,
259	 * and the process binding it is proof the game server itself came up" — see its
260	 * own comment. For most families that port is also the join port, so the
261	 * distinction never mattered. For the eight below it is an RCON/query/admin
262	 * port, and `GAME_PORT`'s own inline comments have always said so.
263	 *
264	 * It started mattering the moment provisioning began auto-forwarding "the game's
265	 * own port" for NAT servers using this same map. Found live 2026-09-06 by
266	 * provisioning a real Rust server on node-2: the guest listened correctly on
267	 * 28015/udp (join) and 28016/tcp (RCON), the node's NAT had exactly one game
268	 * rule — 28016/tcp — and the dashboard handed the customer that RCON port as
269	 * their connect address. No player could ever have joined. That is the identical
270	 * outage found on the real paying customer `rust-w75hko` (see
271	 * docs/DOCUMENTATION.md's node migration section), whose root cause was
272	 * previously read as "allocateGameForward was never called for it"; it is called,
273	 * just with the wrong port.
274	 *
275	 * Every entry is sourced from the family's own `docker run -p ...` mapping in
276	 * prisma/catalog.ts / the seed-wave*-games.ts files — the only ports docker
277	 * actually exposes off the container — cross-checked against the join port
278	 * `GAME_PORT`'s own comment already names. Anything NOT listed here joins on its
279	 * `GAME_PORT` entry; use {@link joinPortFor} rather than reading this directly.
280	 */
281	const GAME_JOIN_PORT_OVERRIDE: Partial<Record<GameFamily, { port: number; protocol: "tcp" | "udp" }>> = {
282	  rust: { port: 28015, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 28016/tcp rcon
283	  ark: { port: 7777, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27020/tcp rcon
284	  projectzomboid: { port: 16261, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27015/tcp rcon
285	  factorio: { port: 34197, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27015/tcp rcon
286	  arkasa: { port: 7777, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27020/tcp rcon
287	  // (soulmask needs no entry any more: its GAME_PORT is now 8777/udp — the port
288	  //  players join on — because its 18888/tcp admin port turned out to be bound
289	  //  to loopback inside the container and unreachable. See GAME_PORT.)
290	  squad: { port: 7787, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 21114/tcp rcon
291	  kf2: { port: 7777, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 8080/tcp webadmin
292	  // Source-engine families: srcds binds the SAME port number on both protocols,
293	  // and the two are different services. UDP 27015 is the game + A2S query
294	  // protocol players and server browsers speak; TCP 27015 is RCON. Proven live
295	  // on a running Garry's Mod server 2026-09-07 — an A2S_INFO datagram to UDP
296	  // 27015 answered `ff ff ff ff 41 …` (S2C_CHALLENGE), while TCP 27015 accepted
297	  // the connection and returned nothing at all to the same query. Because the
298	  // port NUMBERS match, this one hid where the others didn't: the forward looked
299	  // right and was on the wrong protocol, so players could not connect AND the
300	  // single port left published to the internet was RCON — the exact exposure
301	  // `196e5c9` was written to end.
302	  gmod: { port: 27015, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27015/tcp rcon
303	  // 7 Days to Die is the same shape as the Source families above — it binds
304	  // 26900 on BOTH protocols and only the UDP one carries the game. Verified
305	  // live 2026-09-07: the server's own log says `[NET] Disabling protocol:
306	  // SteamNetworking` then `NET: LiteNetLib server started`, and LiteNetLib is
307	  // UDP-only; an A2S_INFO datagram to udp:26900 answered `ff ff ff ff 41 …`
308	  // (S2C_CHALLENGE) while tcp:26900 accepted the connection and replied with
309	  // four unrelated ASCII bytes. Matching port numbers hid this exactly the way
310	  // they hid it for Garry's Mod.
311	  sdtd: { port: 26900, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 26900/tcp
312	  tf2: { port: 27015, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27015/tcp rcon
313	  l4d2: { port: 27015, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27015/tcp rcon
314	  cs2: { port: 27015, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27015/tcp rcon
315	  // (unturned needs no entry: its GAME_PORT is already 27015/udp — the same port
316	  //  players join on — because Unturned binds no TCP port at all. See GAME_PORT.)
317	};

319	/**
320	 * The port a player's game client actually connects to for this family — the
321	 * one that must be port-forwarded for a NAT server and shown to the customer as
322	 * their connect address. Identical to {@link GAME_PORT} for every family except
323	 * the eight in `GAME_JOIN_PORT_OVERRIDE`.
324	 */

326	  return GAME_JOIN_PORT_OVERRIDE[family] ?? GAME_PORT[family];

1	import { REGION_LABELS, REGION_COUNTRY } from "@/lib/node-regions";
2	import { APP } from "@/lib/nx/sprites";
3	import { GAME_ART_SLUG, type GameFamily } from "@/lib/games";
4	
5	/* Presentation data for the deploy wizard.
6	 *
7	 * The rule this file exists to enforce: NOTHING PRICED LIVES HERE. The design
8	 * sandbox kept plans, add-on rates and term discounts in a catalog like this and
9	 * did the arithmetic in the browser. In the real system every one of those
10	 * numbers has an owner — Plan/GamePlan/HostingPlan/EmailPlan rows, and
11	 * `orderQuote` for anything derived — and a second copy here would be a second
12	 * pricing formula that silently drifts from the one that charges the card.
13	 *
14	 * What IS allowed here is data that has no source anywhere else and cannot be
15	 * wrong in a way that costs money: where a datacentre sits on a globe, which
16	 * artwork a service tile uses, how far a disk slider steps.
17	 */
18	
19	/** Formatting only. Cents in, string out; no arithmetic beyond the divide. */
20	export const money = (cents: number) =>
21	  "$" + (cents / 100).toLocaleString("en-US", { minimumFractionDigits: 2, maximumFractionDigits: 2 });
22	
23	export type Region = {
24	  key: string;
25	  name: string;
26	  area: string;
27	  flag: string;
28	  /** Degrees, for the orthographic globe in the region step. */
29	  lat: number;
30	  lon: number;
31	  /**
32	   * The enabled nodes sitting in this region. The order intent wants a specific
33	   * `nodeId`, but the design asks the customer for a REGION — so the wizard
34	   * resolves one from here. Without this the intent would carry no node and the
35	   * platform's scheduler would place the server on RAM headroom alone, silently
36	   * ignoring the location the customer just chose.
37	   */
38	  nodeIds: string[];
39	  /**
40	   * NOMINAL round-trip, milliseconds. This is an indicative figure for the
41	   * region, NOT a measurement of the customer's own connection — nothing on the
42	   * platform probes latency per visitor. It exists so the picker can rank
43	   * locations sensibly; it must never be presented as "your" latency.
44	   */
45	  ms: number;
46	};
47	
48	/* Keyed by the platform's REAL datacentre codes (lib/node-regions.ts), not an
49	   invented set — the wizard offers a region only where a Node actually exists,
50	   so the picker can never sell a location we cannot provision in. Coordinates
51	   are the only thing added here; the labels and flags come from the shared map
52	   so this file cannot drift from it. */
53	const COORDS: Record<string, { lat: number; lon: number; area: string; ms: number }> = {
54	  sgp1: { lat: 1.35, lon: 103.82, area: "Asia", ms: 12 },
55	  bhs1: { lat: 45.31, lon: -73.87, area: "North America", ms: 62 },

content.thinking:
Since all families have posters but only kf2 lacks hero art, I'm thinking I should filter the hero rotation to families that actually have hero images available, since fs access is possible in this server component context. Curating which families appear in a featured rotation feels like a reasonable design choice rather than the kind of hardcoded stat I want to avoid.

Now I'm thinking about how to make each card's glow reflect its poster's actual colors rather than a fixed palette. Server-side pixel extraction would need a JPEG decoder like sharp, so I'm leaning toward a client-side approach instead — drawing the poster into a canvas and sampling the average color from the pixel data, which genuinely pulls the tint from the artwork itself.

I'll cache the sampled colors per poster in a module-level map so each is only computed once, downsampling the canvas and weighting toward saturated pixels before converting to HSL and boosting saturation/lightness into a richer range. For a good default state before images load, I'm also seeding a deterministic fallback hue from each game's title string, then swapping in the real sampled color once the image finishes loading.

Actually, sharp is already included in Next.js 15's default serverExternalPackages list, and specifying the option appends to rather than replaces those defaults, so sharp should still work fine.

Since I can't run a build to verify, and I want zero risk, a safer route is to pre-extract the palette with a script now and write the results into a static data module inside the app folder — real colors sampled from the actual key art, documented with how to regenerate them. This avoids any runtime native dependency, gives instant color availability with no flash, and fits the art-directed brief since it's per-title color derived from the actual artwork rather than a hardcoded statistic.

I'm designing the sampling algorithm: resize each poster down, convert pixels to HSL, filter out near-black/near-white/low-saturation pixels, then bucket hues weighted by saturation and a mid-lightness preference to find the dominant hue, average its values, and clamp saturation/lightness into a usable range for a glowing color on a dark background. Before writing this, I want to follow the required two-pass process — draft a short design plan first, then review and revise it — so I'm sketching that plan now under a working concept I'm calling "Arcade," a premium visual direction to guide the palette and layout choices.

Now I'm working out the specific palette: a near-black ground, a slightly raised dark card tone, a warm off-white for text instead of pure white, a hot editorial accent color, and a metallic tone for pricing details, plus a per-poster tint sampled from the algorithm. I'm also weighing display, body, and mono typefaces that fit the maximalist, art-directed magazine feel I'm going for.

Now critiquing my own pass: I realize the hot orange-on-black plus metallic combo reads as a generic esports/energy-drink template and would clash with letting each poster's own tint carry the color. I decide to pull back the global accent to something more restrained — a warm paper tone paired sparingly with a single deep oxblood/lacquer red — so the saturated color on screen comes only from the individual poster tints.

Actually, Bricolage Grotesque has become a bit of an AI-site cliché now, so I should reconsider. Familjen Grotesk feels too trendy, Instrument Serif would collide with the editorial-serif concept, Archivo was already used in v1 — but Anton, the bold poster/newsstand face, has real confident presence worth exploring.

Considering more options: Bebas Neue is overused on gaming thumbnails, Chivo and Sora feel flat, League Gothic isn't on Google Fonts, Oswald is too common. But Big Shoulders Display stands out — condensed, athletic, poster-like with variable weights, genuinely reads as magazine masthead rather than sci-fi or gamer. I'm settling on it as the display voice for the masthead.

There's a risk though: at huge sizes with a dark background, tall condensed caps might slide into "esports poster" territory. I can mitigate that by using mixed case, generous tracking, a bone-paper color, and real editorial hierarchy — kicker, deck, byline rules — rather than all-caps neon. But reconsidering again, premium console storefront spreads often lean toward wide heavy grotesques rather than condensed ones, so I'm weighing alternatives like Archivo Expanded, Anybody, Darker Grotesque, and Familjen Grotesk before ultimately committing back to Big Shoulders.

I'm settling on Big Shoulders Display as the masthead — decisive and dense enough for a maximalist layout, and distinct from anything else considered. For the body I want something warm so the page feels printed rather than screen-native, ruling out Fraunces for conflicting with the editorial concept and passing on plainer options like Public Sans or Hanken Grotesk in favor of Instrument Sans, which has just enough character in its letterforms. For numerals and specs I'm choosing DM Mono to give price and spec blocks that magazine tech-sidebar feel.

Now I'm second-guessing the brass accent color for prices, since it reads too much like a luxury watch site — I'll drop it in favor of setting prices in DM Mono with the tint reserved for currency marks and kickers, replacing brass with a graphite hairline instead. I'm also worried the card-heavy layout risks looking like a generic SaaS grid, so I'm reworking it into a magazine-spread structure with deliberately unequal blocks, starting with a full-bleed hero.

Below that, a draggable poster strip lets users tilt and select titles to swap the hero art and price block — the moment where picking a game should feel satisfying. The second section, "The rack," goes maximalist with a dense wall of all 42 posters and genre filter tabs, where hovering lifts a poster to reveal its cheapest tier's specs. A third editorial section pairs a bold pull-quote layout with feature details in a two-column spread.

I map out the fourth section as a closing "now playing" band with CTA and two region plates, giving four sections plus hero — matching the brief's 3-4 section requirement. For interactions, I'm settling on spring-eased pointer-tilt with sheen that respects reduced motion, a 40px drag threshold, and poster-lift reveals that work via keyboard focus and touch tap, all while keeping stats honest like the real 45,761 mod count.

I add the required trademark disclaimer to the poster wall footer clarifying Nxeon isn't affiliated with game studios, and note entrance animations must run on load as CSS rather than being scroll-gated. I'm also flagging a key change from pass one: dropping the hot-orange/brass accent palette since it read as generic esports styling and clashed with per-title tints, in favor of a neutral bone/ash/graphite chrome.

Now I'm defining the final color palette — deep ink and pitch grounds, a slab-toned card background, warm bone for primary text, and a muted ash for secondary text — while also swapping Bricolage Grotesque for Big Shoulders Display since Bricolage now reads as an AI-generated-site cliché, and restructuring the layout from an even grid into an asymmetric magazine spread anchored by a full catalogue "rack."

That gives me five named hex values plus per-card sampled tint, matching the brief's request for colour pulled from game art rather than a single global accent — a neutral chrome base is the right call here. # v8 "Arcade" — design plan

## PASS 1 (first draft)
Palette: --ink #07070A, --slab #101018, --bone #F4F1EA, --ember #FF4D2E, --brass #C8A96A, per-title --tint
Type: Bricolage Grotesque (display), Instrument Sans (text), DM Mono (numbers)
Layout: full-bleed hero + 3-col card grid of featured games + feature strip + pricing cards

## PASS 2 — SELF REVIEW, what changed and why

1. KILLED the hot-orange `--ember` and the `--brass` metallic entirely.
   - #FF4D2E on near-black + gold is the default esports/energy-drink palette AND
     the default "bold Framer editorial" palette. Twice generic.
   - Worse: a single saturated global accent would DROWN the per-title poster
     tints, which the concept says are supposed to be the colour source.
   - Replaced with: fully neutral chrome (ink / slab / bone / ash / hairline) and
     ZERO chromatic global accent. 100% of the chroma on the page comes from
     colour sampled out of the real key art. This is what a premium console
     storefront actually does — neutral shelf, colour from the box art.
   - The primary CTA therefore becomes bone-paper-on-dark (a printed card on a
     dark page), which is a more expensive move than a coloured button anyway.

2. DROPPED Bricolage Grotesque. It has become as much of an "AI-generated site"
   tell in 2025 as Space Grotesk. Replaced with **Big Shoulders** (variable,
   opsz + wght axes) — a tall condensed newsstand/masthead face with real
   personality at 100px+, and emphatically not a sci-fi/gamer face.
   De-risking it away from "esports poster": set in MIXED CASE at weight 500–800
   with in-line weight contrast, on warm paper-bone, with editorial leading —
   never all-caps neon.

3. Prices set in brass -> prices set in DM Mono bone, with only the small "from"
   kicker taking the card's tint. Brass removed.

4. Restructured the layout away from an even 3-col card grid (that reads
   marketplace-SaaS) into a MAGAZINE SPREAD with deliberately unequal blocks,
   and made the maximalist flex an actual full catalogue wall rather than 6
   hero cards.

## FINAL

Palette (5 named + 1 hairline + per-title tint):
  --v8-ink   #08080b   page ground
  --v8-well  #040406   full-bleed art wells, footer
  --v8-slab  #12121a   card ground
  --v8-bone  #f2eee6   warm paper, primary type + inverted CTA card
  --v8-ash   #9c9aa6   secondary type
  --v8-hair  rgba(242,238,230,.12)
  --tint     per-title, SAMPLED from that title's poster with sharp (server side,
             dominant saturated hue bucket, clamped S .46-.74 / L .55-.68)

Type (3 roles):
  Big Shoulders   (variable, opsz axis) — masthead / title plates / section heads
  Instrument Sans — decks, body prose
  DM Mono 300/400/500 — kickers, specs, prices, region data

Layout:
  HERO "the marquee"   — full-bleed 16:9 key art of the selected title, oversized
                         masthead ("42 worlds. / Online in 47 seconds."), a feature
                         plate with that title's real cheapest tier, and a
                         DRAGGABLE bottom rail of 14 posters that tilt under the
                         pointer and swap the backdrop when picked.
  2 "the rack"         — all 42 titles with an active plan as a dense poster wall,
                         genre tabs, each poster tilts + lifts + reveals its real
                         plan specs.
  3 "the spec sheet"   — editorial two-up: display-scale statement + prose against
                         a mono spec table of real DB figures, then the two region
                         plates (Singapore / Germany) with honest RTT labelling.
  4 closing band       — the real mod-catalogue count + a marquee of the modded
                         titles, against an inverted bone paper CTA card. Footer
                         carries the trademark notice.

content.thinking:
Now I'm planning the full v8.css structure, scoping everything under `.v8` with tokens, base resets, shared primitives like kickers and buttons, and then the major components: marquee, rack, sheet, and closing sections.

For visual polish I'm adding a fixed film-grain overlay using an SVG noise texture with soft-light blending, a full-height hero marquee with a slow ken-burns drift on the active image guarded by reduced-motion preferences, and layered gradient scrims for legibility.

I'm building a color-mix based bloom accent that shifts with the theme tint, plus a three-column top bar with brand, nav, and actions floating over the artwork without a hard border.

Now I'm sizing the logo image with a fixed height and auto width so it stays crisp with next/image, then laying out the masthead grid with a wide headline column and a narrower side column, and defining the display font styling for the headline with variable font weight and optical size settings.

For the two-line headline, I'm giving the emphasized number in line one a bold 800 weight while the surrounding text sits lighter around 350-380, and making line two fully bold to create contrast between the lines.

I'm adding a subtle text-shadow so the headline stays legible over the background art, then styling the deck copy in Instrument Sans with generous line-height and a constrained width, and defining the button base styles with a monospace uppercase label treatment.

Deciding uppercase mono buttons read editorial rather than gamer, keeping that direction. Now I'm sketching button variants — a paper-toned solid, a ghost outline, and a tint variant using color-mix for hover states.

Setting dark text on tint backgrounds for legibility, adding an ink button variant for the paper card, a large-size variant, and picking a crisp 2px radius for the editorial feel. Now defining the kicker label style with mono uppercase text, wide letter-spacing, and an accompanying dot marker.

For the feature plate, I'm building a dark layered gradient panel with blur/backdrop-filter, hairline borders (one tinted on top), layered shadows for depth, and rounded corners — then adding a tint-based glow effect on top.

I'm also sizing the logo image inside the plate, but realizing the source PNGs have lots of transparent padding around the actual logo, so a small fixed height like 54px would shrink the visible mark too much. I'm adjusting to a wider box with more generous height, around 80x260px, using object-fit contain and left-aligned positioning to give the logo more visual presence.

I want to check the actual trimmed bounding boxes of the logo PNGs to see how much padding they really have before finalizing sizing. Then I'm defining the surrounding UI details: mono uppercase chip labels with hairline borders, a spec grid with hairline dividers and mono key/value styling, and a price display using a distinct display typeface.

Actually correcting myself — the price numbers should be mono at 26-28px, weight 500, with mono uppercase currency/label text around it. Now writing the rail label and wrap styles...

For the horizontal rail itself, I'm making it a flex scroll container with drag-to-scroll behavior, hiding the scrollbar, and adding a grabbing cursor state — but I'll skip disabling pointer-events on children since that could interfere with pointer capture during drag, using user-select:none instead.

Now I'm styling the card items in the rail: fixed-width flex items with the image poster showing a 2:3 aspect ratio, rounded corners, and a subtle border, plus an active state that highlights the selected card with a tinted border, glow, and a slight lift and width increase.

Actually growing width on click could shift scroll, so I switch to a scale-and-lift transform instead to avoid layout shift, adding a slight saturation boost. I'm also setting typography for the name and price labels, and considering dimming inactive cards to about 62% opacity while keeping them above the never-fully-transparent threshold, though I'm second-guessing whether dimming posters is the right storefront feel.

Now I'm settling on 68% as a safer dim level, then writing a sheen overlay effect that tracks cursor position with a radial gradient highlight blended in screen mode, activated on hover or focus.

For the tilt effect, I'm using 3D perspective transforms with custom properties for rotation, lift, and scale, with different transition speeds for hover versus active dragging states. I'm realizing that applying `will-change: transform` globally across 42 cards is too costly for performance, so I want to scope it to only trigger on hover instead.

Now I'm moving on to building the rack section's styles, setting up the dark background container with responsive padding and a two-column header grid, then defining the heading typography with a variable font and fluid sizing.

Still writing tab styles... I'm also setting up the rack grid with auto-fill columns and making sure to use content-start/items-start so rows don't stretch to match the tallest sibling.

Writing card typography styles...

Now I'm reconsidering the panel positioning — it needs to overlay the bottom of the poster shot itself rather than sit below with the name plate, since the shot's overflow-hidden clipping is what creates the slide-up reveal effect.

Adding panel styles and hover transitions...

Actually, position static would break the aspect-ratio box on touch devices, so I'll keep the panel absolute and just always reveal it via translateY(0) on hover-none screens, which permanently shows the info over the poster. I also need to adjust the spec grid to drop to 2 columns on narrow cards so it doesn't feel cramped.

Adding stretch link and focus styles...

Adding sheet layout styles...

Adding sticky positioning to the spec table with align-self start for grid compatibility, then styling the row layout with flexbox spacing and dashed dividers between entries...

Styling region cards and headers...

I'm reasoning through the exception of using a bold display face for the big headline number while keeping DM Mono reserved for spec values elsewhere — a deliberate contrast rule. Then I'm defining a lighter-weight subheading style to sit under that heavy number for visual contrast, and starting on the paper card's background and text color styles.

Continuing the paper card styling with shadow, border, and inner label/heading/paragraph rules...

Writing scrolling filmstrip animation...

Now I'm building the footer styles with a top row containing the logo mark and navigation links, separated by a hairline border.

I'm defining the legal text block and setting up responsive breakpoints that collapse the multi-column layouts to single columns at smaller widths, along with reduced-motion accessibility handling.

The panel reveal still works instantly under reduced motion since it's an interaction trigger, not a decorative animation, and it stays hidden until hover/focus while always visible on touch. The only opacity-zero content is deliberate alternate backdrop layers in a cross-fade stack, not actual hidden content, so that's safe too.

Checking that everything renders correctly with JS disabled: the Marquee SSRs with the first title's art and full rail visible, and the Rack SSRs with all titles shown — tabs and selection won't function but nothing is missing from view. Now I'm adding a subtle grain overlay texture using a fixed, pointer-events-none pseudo-element with low opacity and overlay blend mode.

The full-viewport grain with blend mode should give that desired printed texture over the paper card, though I want to keep the opacity low for performance. Now I'm adding a subtle drift animation to the marquee art, scaling and shifting it slowly for a living, breathing feel while respecting reduced-motion preferences.

I'm making sure the image fades in smoothly and adding a fallback tinted radial gradient behind it so there's always a colored field even before the image loads, keeping the plate and masthead readable throughout.

Bigger problem though: the `.v8-btn-paper`, `.v8-btn-ink`, and `.v8-btn-tint` buttons are rendering with invisible text because `.v8 a { color: inherit }` has higher specificity than the button color rules, so text inherits from the parent background instead of using the intended contrast color — that's why buttons appear as empty boxes.

The real fix is wrapping the base resets in `:where()` so they always lose to any other selector — that's the robust solution worth calling out explicitly. content.text:
Everything verified and the sandbox is torn down. Here's the report.

## What I built

All files in `/opt/nxeon/app/newwebsitev8/` — nothing outside it was touched (verified with `find -newermt`):

| File | Lines | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `layout.tsx` | 85 | fonts, `robots: {index:false}`, `<div className="v8 …">` |
| `page.tsx` | 372 | Server Component, `force-dynamic`, all DB reads |
| `v8.css` | 1609 | every rule scoped under `.v8` (verified by grep) |
| `art.ts` | 184 | server-only: key-art lookup + `sharp` colour sampling |
| `types.ts` | 63 | shared shapes, plain module |
| `icons.tsx` | 99 | 8 SVG icons, **no `"use client"`**, individual named exports |
| `tilt.ts` | 88 | `"use client"` — pointer-tilt/sheen hook |
| `Marquee.tsx` | 333 | `"use client"` — hero + draggable rail |
| `Rack.tsx` | 174 | `"use client"` — 42-poster wall + genre tabs |

Hero + 3 sections: **the marquee** (full-bleed key art, oversized masthead, live feature plate, 14-poster draggable rail), **the rack** (all 42 titles, genre tabs, lift-and-reveal), **the spec sheet** (editorial two-up + mono figure table + the two region plates), **closing band** (real mod count + marquee strip + inverted paper CTA).

## Design plan, and what self-review changed

**Pass 1:** ink/slab/bone + hot `--ember #FF4D2E` + `--brass #C8A96A`; Bricolage Grotesque / Instrument Sans / DM Mono; 3-col card grid.

**Four things the review killed:**
1. **Removed the hot-orange accent and the brass entirely.** Orange-on-black + gold is simultaneously the default esports palette *and* the default "bold Framer editorial" palette — generic twice. Worse, a saturated global accent would have drowned the per-title poster tints the concept is built on. Replaced with **zero chromatic global accent**: chrome is neutral warm-paper, and 100% of the chroma is sampled from the real key art. Side benefit — the primary CTA became bone-paper-on-dark, a more expensive move than a coloured button.
2. **Dropped Bricolage Grotesque** — as much an AI-site tell now as Space Grotesk. Replaced with **Big Shoulders** (variable, `opsz` + `wght`), a newsstand masthead face; de-risked away from esports by setting it mixed-case at 380/820 with in-line weight contrast, never all-caps neon.
3. **Prices out of brass, into DM Mono bone**; only the small "from" kicker takes the tint.
4. **Restructured from an even card grid into an unequal magazine spread**, and made the maximalist flex the *entire* catalogue wall rather than six hero cards.

Final palette: `--v8-ink #08080b`, `--v8-well #040406`, `--v8-slab #12121a`, `--v8-bone #f2eee6`, `--v8-ash #9c9aa6`, `--v8-hair rgba(242,238,230,.12)`, plus per-title `--tint`.

## Colour comes from the art

`art.ts` downsamples each poster to 40×54 with `sharp`, discards near-black/white/grey, buckets by hue weighted by saturation² × mid-lightness proximity, and clamps S to .46–.74 / L to .55–.68 (unclamped it returns hazard-lights like `#f51b0a`). 5ms per poster, 220ms for all 44, memoised per process, lazy `import()` inside try/catch with a neutral graphite fallback. Verified working: picking Satisfactory turns its CTA and chip border orange; Factorio's rack card glows orange; ARK's blue.

## Verified

Built an **isolated copy of the tree in the scratchpad** (node_modules/public symlinked) and ran `next dev` on :3055 — I did **not** build or run dev in `/opt/nxeon`, per the build-isolation rule. Confirmed afterwards: prod `.next` untouched, prod still 200 on :3000, sandbox deleted (symlinks removed first).

- `npx tsc --noEmit` from `/opt/nxeon` → **exit 0, whole repo clean**
- Page renders 200; **0 page errors, 0 non-CSP console errors** (the CSP errors are the root layout's Meta/Google tags, identical on `/newwebsitev1`)
- Interaction tests passed: plain click selects; **6px jiggle still counts as a click**; a real drag scrolls (0→216px) and does **not** hijack selection; keyboard focus reveals the spec panel (`translateY=0`); genre tabs filter 42→7; **no readable text at opacity < .15**; under `reducedMotion: reduce` the tilt hook writes nothing and the marquee animation is `none`
- Desktop 1560px and mobile 390px both reviewed by screenshot and iterated on

**Two real bugs I hit and fixed:**
- My base resets written as `.v8 a { color: inherit }` / `.v8 p { margin: 0 }` carry specificity **(0,1,1)** and were outranking every component class (0,1,0) regardless of order — the primary CTA rendered as an **empty white box** (bone-on-bone) and *every* `margin-top` was dropped, collapsing the page's vertical rhythm. Fixed by wrapping all resets in `:where()`. Same family as the repo's documented `.card{position:relative}` vs `lg:absolute` trap, but inside one authored stylesheet.
- `Big_Shoulders` logged `⨯ Failed to find font override values` on every render (Google renamed it from "Big Shoulders Display" and next/font has no metrics entry under the new name). Fixed with `adjustFontFallback: false`; fallback stacks live in the CSS.

- **Game prices changed in prod mid-session** — a ~20% reduction across `GamePlan` *and* `Plan`, plus `introPriceCents` now populated. My first probe read $5.38–$53.98; the page now renders $4.30–$43.18 and VPS from $12.78. Not a bug — it proves the page reads live. Whoever made that change may want to know.
- **Intro pricing is deliberately not shown.** `GamePlan.introPriceCents` now exists, but a first-term price needs a "renews at $X" disclosure; I show the regular/renewal rate, which can only over-state. Worth an owner decision if this concept wins.
- **The production cookie banner physically covers the hero rail** on a first visit (it's fixed to the viewport bottom, exactly where the rail sits). This cost me 20 minutes of false test failures. It affects all four concepts equally and I left the design alone, but it's a real first-impression problem for any bottom-anchored hero element.
- `public/logos/steam.svg`, `counterstrike.svg` and `wine.svg` are **also 0 bytes**, not just `caddy.svg`. This page references none of them.
- Posters are **2:3 (300×450)**, not the 3:4 the brief stated. I used 2/3. Title logotypes are 640×360 with alpha and trimmed ratios from 0.5:1 (V Rising) to 6:1 (Factorio), so the plate sets a width and lets height follow.
- `kf2` has a poster but **no hero art**; `stationeers` is an active family with **no `-server-hosting` route** (it's outside `ACTIVE_GAME_FAMILIES`). Both are handled — the shelf self-heals, stationeers links to `/game-servers`.

## Not verified

- **No production build.** As instructed I didn't run `npm run build`, so this is verified under `next dev` only. The one prod-build-specific risk is `sharp`; I confirmed it's in Next 15's default `server-external-packages.json`, and it's imported lazily inside try/catch, so the worst case is neutral grey tints rather than a failure.
- No real touch device — the `(hover: none)` path (rack panel renders open, sheen off) was reasoned about and coded but only exercised via viewport emulation.
- The dev overlay shows "1 Issue" on my route, but it shows the identical overlay state on `/newwebsitev1`, so it's a pre-existing root-layout hydration mismatch, not mine.
